extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers, playwrights, and adaptors interested in story structure and craft
extracted.subtask_description: Using Aristotle’s taxonomy (plot, character, idea, dialogue, music, spectacle) as a practical tool to critique, structure, and rewrite narrative work across media; includes modes (lyric/epic/dramatic), scene-purpose mapping, and an exercise to reorder elements and rewrite. Useful for writers and theater adaptors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristotle's six elements of story
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle’s elements of tragedy (generalized to story): in descending importance — plot, character, idea, dialogue, music, spectacle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a taxonomy and paradigm to analyze and think about how a story is working. The podcast notes the original ordering and that Aristotle frames this as a descriptive ranking of importance, but it functions as a useful checklist of what a story can contain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose and prioritize the elements for your work
rubrics_metrics.description: Each story has its own order of importance for the six elements; the Aristotle order is not prescriptive for every story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rank the six elements for the piece you’re writing (which is most important, which least). Be deliberate about which elements you emphasize and organize your scenes and structure to serve that prioritized list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scenes must serve a clear element-purpose (e.g., fight scenes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify what a scene is doing — a fight scene can be plot, character, or spectacle — and write it to fulfill that role rather than assuming spectacle alone will suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a scene is spectacle-heavy, embed plot or character if you need reader engagement. The podcast gives examples (fight scenes, Jackie Chan) where spectacle is entertaining only when it also supports other elements like geography, character, or plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overdoing one element in your opening
rubrics_metrics.description: Openings often overemphasize a single element (character-driven or voice-driven), which can create an unfulfilled promise if the rest of the work prioritizes different elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Donald Maass’s breakdown: character-driven openings ground reader in who and where (plot + character); voice-driven openings foreground language/ideas/music. Make sure the opening’s dominant element aligns with what the rest of the book delivers so you don’t ‘impress and not fulfill.’

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish voice/music from dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Music refers to the lyrical quality or beautiful sentence-level writing; dialogue is the spoken interaction of characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that what you value (lyrical language vs. conversation) occupies different elements. Some readers are attracted to music/voice while others prefer plot/character/dialogue; don’t conflate them and design the work knowing which you prioritize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of narration: lyric, epic, dramatic
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle’s three modes describe the author/audience relationship: lyric (author telling own experience), epic (author telling a story that happens to someone else), dramatic (showing story without author’s presence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and choose mode(s) deliberately. Modes can be mixed in any medium. Use mode awareness to decide how present the author is, whether to use narrator devices, and how you expect the audience to engage mentally with the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium and audience expectations determine element emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Different media tend to privilege different elements: novels often excel at plot and ideas, TV often leans character/plot, film leans spectacle, theater uses music and spectacle differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider your medium and intended audience when ordering elements; what your audience expects will shape which elements you should prioritize. Examples: Aaron Sorkin (dialogue-driven TV); Phantom of the Opera (music/spectacle for certain audiences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptations may require introducing or elevating elements
rubrics_metrics.description: When adapting source material that lacks a dominant element (e.g., a coffee-table book without plot), you must add or elevate elements to suit the target medium/audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: adapting a photo book into a play required the adaptor to create plot and lace the show with music. Be prepared to change the order of elements to make the adaptation succeed in its new medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activate audience imagination for fantastical or staged elements
rubrics_metrics.description: For fantasy or stage presentations that can’t present literal realism, you must create a narrative mode or collaborative creation mode so the audience will 'imagine this with me.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques include narrator devices, puppetry, or other framing that signals to the audience to co-create the story. This keeps suspension of disbelief intact (Penn & Teller, puppetry examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid letting dramatic mode remove audience engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Overreliance on dramatic mode (simply showing everything) can let the audience 'off the hook' and reduce their imaginative participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance showing with devices that require audience imaginative work; television and film can make this harder because audiences are less primed to do creative work while watching, so you may need framing to recruit their imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make deliberate promises and fulfill them across the work
rubrics_metrics.description: If you foreground certain elements early (e.g., gorgeous language, spectacle), the rest of the work should continue to honor or integrate those elements; otherwise readers feel misled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read submissions or your own opening with an eye for what promise is being made and ensure subsequent sections deliver matching emphasis or reconcile the shift intentionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical exercise: rank, reorder, rewrite
rubrics_metrics.description: An actionable exercise given: take something you’ve written, rank the six elements for that piece, reorder the elements, and rewrite the piece to match the new ranking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This exercise forces you to see what element your piece currently prioritizes and to practice reshaping a piece to foreground a different element (useful for development and learning how element emphasis changes effect).
